utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. I see that Mr. Stewart is not in.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. He won't be here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So for the Defence today we have Ms. Loukas and Ms. Cmeric; and for the Prosecution, we have Mr. Tieger and Mr. Hannis. But we first have to know in what case. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. On the programme today is, as a result of some conversations yesterday between the parties, the examination of Mr. Fazlovic to be finished, and then we'll stop, but not before having dealt with the documents in respect of Mr. Treanor. If there's nothing else on the agenda -- yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing else. Yes. Madam Usher, would you then, please, escort Mr. Fazlovic into the courtroom. Perhaps I should ask you whether the conversation of yesterday also resulted in another statement of Mr. Fazlovic as far as redactions are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. I've received a further corrected copy, both in English and B/C/S, from Mr. Hannis this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means that P71 is not the one we thought it would be, but we have a new version. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fazlovic. Before we resume, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Yes. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Hannis: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, if at any time you need to have a copy of your statement in front of you, please let me know and we'll provide that to you. When we left off yesterday, you were telling us about when Mirko Blagojevic and a group of his soldiers came to the fire station and separated you and the other Muslim firemen from the Serb firemen. Can you tell us what happened after they took you outside and physically beat you. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they identified us as Muslims, they started to beat us in the corridor of the firehouse and mistreat us in other manner. Then this person by the name of Dragan wanted to kill us all. He said: You should all be killed. And then Mirko Blagojevic said, after someone had told him, that we should go to the police station, which is located about 500 metres from the firehouse. They told us to put our hands behind our head like this, and then they escorted us down the main road, down the main street. The man who led us kept beating us with his rubber baton. As we were walking down the main street, we noticed armed groups leading other people from the side streets. We were being taken towards the police station; I don't know where they were taking them. We came across one more group of armed and uniformed soldiers who asked our leader who we were, and he said that we were snipers from the fire brigade and that he was taking us to the SUP, to the police station. And then this other man said: Just move away. I'll kill them right here on the spot. But our leader then said: Mirko told us to take them to the police station. When we came close to the police station, I noticed, near the Borovo shop, a friend of mine who used to work with me at the fire station. He was wearing a military uniform. He just bent his head down and said nothing. When we came close to the SUP building, some five or six metres away from the building, we saw a group of soldiers who formed two lines, two rows, through which we had to pass, and they kept beating us as we were going inside the police station. I saw a number of people covered with blood in the police station. When we got in, they told us to form a line and face the wall. They kept us there for half an hour, like this, verbally abused us, and at one point they told us to turn around. And when we turned around, we saw that the whole station was in a state of chaos. There were many soldiers there. I noticed Veselic among them. Veselic was a secondary school teacher, I think. He was the one who was inspecting some papers. Once again they wanted us to show them our IDs. There was a small reception box at the SUP which was now covered with paper. There was only a small window through which someone was observing us. Police officers continued to mistreat us. They made fun of us. They put some sort of green beret on our head and accused us of being Ustashas or Green Berets. We tried to tell them that we were simply doing our job, that we had nothing against the army and that that's why we stayed, because we believed that they would protect us, as we had been told initially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me stop you there for a second, Mr. Fazlovic. And Dragan Veselic, who you saw in the police station, do you know what his position was in the police department?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he did not work for the police, so I'm not sure I can tell you with certainty what his position was in the SUP. But he must have been someone important, because he was making decisions. He must have been some sort of police commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he tell you and your fellow firemen what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said we should all be taken to Luka and that we should all be killed. Other soldiers followed suit and they kept saying: You balijas should never return. You're finished. And things like that. So we stood there waiting to be taken to the Luka camp, and then at one point a man arrived, a man whom I didn't know, who had come to Brcko earlier, who -- and he recognised me because I was the president of the union at one point. We had a blockade -- we had blocked a road because of some salaries that had not been paid and that's where he saw me. He had some kind of argument with Veselic and others who were there, and he convinced him that we were still necessary for the town because the town was still on fire, a lot of houses were still burning, and that it would be a good idea for us to be taken back to the firehouse, because we were needed, which Veselic accepted, and he told one of the police officers to take us back to the fire station. However, this police officer, Pudic, instead took us to the Luka camp. I personally knew this police officer, and as we were passing by the Posavina Hotel and the Radnik cinema, I saw a large number of bodies on a pile. I got frightened and said: Pudic, where are you taking us? And he said: I'm taking you to Luka. And I said: Well, this other gentleman told you that should take us back to the police station [as interpreted]. So we somehow managed to convince him to take us back. He had to check something before he eventually took us to the firehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the man who --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man who intervened on your behalf at the police station, was he also a policeman? And if so, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that he was a policeman. Before the war he had been employed there as a traffic police commander. I think his last name was Milic, but I'm not sure. He was either from Orasje or Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you eventually got back to the fire station, were there still soldiers at the fire station?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Soldiers were still there, but there were not that many as initially. Mirko Blagojevic, for instance, was still there, and his entourage, his staff. We had a restaurant at the firehouse, upstairs, and he decided that he would set up his headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once you got back to the fire station, because of the experience that you'd had at the police station, did you make some efforts to contact the JNA garrison to see if you could be sure of some protection?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we came back to the fire station, we were terribly scared. We all shivered. And we asked one of our colleagues from the firehouse to call Pavle Milinkovic, the commander of the JNA garrison, and to ask him if he could perhaps relocate us, if he could move us from there because we simply didn't dare to spend the night with those people inside the firehouse. So this colleague of ours made a phone call in our presence. I think he wanted to speak to the commander, who was not there at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who did he speak to instead?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spoke to Milorad Sehovac. Milorad Sehovac I think was the commander of some sort of special unit within the JNA. Our colleague told us [as interpreted] that we were very frightened, and he asked if there was anything that could be done for us. And the officer said: But why are they scared? Those people are here to defend the Serb people. But then our colleague explained to him that we had been beaten and mistreated. But this officer said: Just nothing. It's good that they are alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 10th of May, about six days after this happened, did you have occasion to see Major Sehovac at the fire station?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On or around that date, a man whom I didn't know arrived. This was Major Sehovac. He was wearing a Serb uniform with army insignia. He was escorted by soldiers, a number of soldiers. There were several of them when they arrived. And he ordered all of us to go outside. He then ordered the group who had worked at the water station - I think there were five or six of them - to get out as well. Then he ordered us to lie down, else he would kill us all. So we complied, and then he said he wanted to know who called Meraje, the Meraje neighbourhood of Brcko. I had no idea what he was talking about. And then he said: Tell me who that was, otherwise I'll kill you all. And then Franjo Vugrincic, a Croat, I believe, spoke up, and he said: Sir, I was the one who called. I couldn't see what was happening. I couldn't see when he got up, because we were all lying down, face down. And he said: Why did you call Meraje? And then he said: My wife is a Serb and this part of town is being shelled, so I was concerned about what was going on. And then he wanted to know why he called Rahici, a village located some seven to eight kilometres from the town, and he said that he had called his former manager, because he wanted to know what to do, because the water tower had been damaged and water was leaking, and he needed instructions. He wanted to know what to do. Then he told him to get up and he told another soldier to take him away and kill him. I believe he also ordered him to take off his shoes. Then we heard a shot. I couldn't see what happened because this was away from where we were and we were still lying down on the ground. He said that this is how all of you will fare if you don't comply. I don't know what exactly happened to this man. All I know that he -- is that he never showed up again. No one ever saw him alive again. We were terribly scared. We were then told to get up. Sehovac saw that I was very frightened and he just tapped me on the shoulder and he said: This is nothing. What are you -- why are you so scared? After which we all went back inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you went back inside, did you hear Major Sehovac give anyone an order about what to do with the man who had been taken away before the gunshot was heard?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said: Take him to Petrovic. Petrovic was in charge of security at the garrison before the war, and he said: Don't let him walk away alive. He will be personally responsible for his life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers who were with the officer, what kind of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers wore regular olive-drab uniforms. One of them had a kind of cap or hat that covered his -- all of his face except his eyes. I didn't recognise any of them. They were not from the town. Whereas this one whose face was hidden must have been a local. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, next I want to direct you to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next I want to direct you to paragraph 23 in your statement, where you talk about a special unit that had been formed. Do you recall a special unit formed by a man named Pedja in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to leading of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the witness has already confirmed that his statement is -- it has been read by him, he has confirmed that this is a correct --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, but if we're going to go through this process of eliciting further evidence in chief from the statement, I think it's appropriate that, particularly in relation to evidence of this nature, that it not be led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis, if you want to elicit any further information from the witness, would you refrain from leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. And could he then be handed a copy of his statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know about this special unit?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special unit was set up quite some time before the war by the JNA. It consisted of people from our town who were notorious for their misbehaviour, were quite problematic characters, and who used to go to Croatia, to Vukovar, and other similar places to fight there over the weekend, after which they would come back. The commander -- or rather, the organiser of this unit was Pedja Bojanic, an architect from Brcko. I once spoke to Ranko Cesic and he told me that he was just sitting there in this unit, doing nothing and receiving a salary, and this is how I know about this unit. And I used to see them around the town wearing red berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything else particular about the uniforms of this special unit that was different from other uniforms of military men around town?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At first, they had very good uniforms, very good quality, camouflage uniforms, brand new. Everything was brand new. The only difference was in the beret they wore, and there was a sign on it. I think it was the number 40 sign or something like that. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had conversations with Ranko Cesic and in paragraph 25 of your statement, you tell us that Mr. Cesic explained that part of his job was to cleanse part of the town. Would you tell the Court what Ranko said about that.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that, together with his group -- the shelling was intense and everybody had run away from the city and those who stayed were hiding in the basement and waiting to see what would happen. Those were innocent people, elderly people, women and children. And he said the job of his unit was to go from house to house. Those were mostly abandoned houses because the first wave of attack had already passed, the first wave of attack by the JNA. So they went from house to house mopping up the terrain, so to speak, to make sure that nobody was left behind, and those left behind were taken to Luka and to Laser, which was a transport enterprise. They were also being taken to Posavina. Their job was to make sure that nobody was left behind, to take everyone away, and to make sure that it was cleansed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during this time when you were told to stay at the fire station until -- or unless you were called out to put out fires, in the course of going around town, doing your job, did you see any evidence of people having been removed from parts of town? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we were being escorted, I noticed that people were being removed from their apartments, houses. They were being taken away by armed people at gunpoint to the police station or elsewhere. Briefly, everybody who was Muslim or Croat was taken to one of these centres to be checked. And a little later, I remember very well when people were being rounded up to be taken to the Batkovici camp. I think that Luka by that time had stopped admitting Muslims and Croats. And they removed everyone who was Croat or Muslim from their residence, put them on buses. This was all done in a very organised way, and I know about it for certain because my uncle had been taken the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that round-up include women and children as well as men?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This round-up for the Batkovici camp involved only men, but at the very beginning of the war, they rounded up everyone: Men and women, to take them to Luka, to Posavina, to the barracks. They would keep the prettier women in Luka. They would rape them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that because Ranko himself told me a couple of times that they had some women back there to whom they referred to as hostesses. He told me they slept on a regular basis with Muslim women who used to be ladies, upper class women, and now were nothing. These women included the wife of a lawyer by the name of Fatic, who was detained and later killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, I want to ask you about a time in -- I think in your statement you say in June or July, when the mosques were destroyed. Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll never forget that day. It was around 2.00 p.m. We were sitting in the fire brigade station: Myself, Mujo Islamovic, Milorad Sekic, Miroslav Pantelic, and some other blokes, when we heard a loud explosion. The walls shook and we were all taken aback, shocked. We wondered what was going on. Very soon afterwards we received a telephone call. The caller told us that the mosque - and I know it was the Sava mosque - was blown up and that we shouldn't go there, but we should go when the wooden mosque burns because of the danger that the fire would spread. I don't remember who it was that said the other two mosques will go up in the air very soon. It was done in an organised, premeditated way. We moved to the next window because we were not able to see the mosque from the window we were sitting by. We heard an explosion and we heard the -- we saw the minaret fall. We went out and, taking the road that goes around the mosques, we went to the health centre, and when we were close to the crossroads near that other mosque, it exploded. We came near and we found soldiers in the courtyard of the Zaim Musanovic school. The soldiers were laughing and merry, and we ran into a man who said: You shouldn't have come now, you should have waited for my call. He told us that we should just stand by and make sure that the fire didn't spread to the health centre or some other building. Not long after that, perhaps half an hour later, people from the SDS came to the scene, including Ranko Ristanic, who at that time was president of the municipality. The name is actually Djordje Ristanic. There was also Nedjo Ilic, head of the health centre, and a man I didn't know who accompanied them. And they talked about this business with the mosques. They said the person who did this used too much explosives, he must have been an amateur because the entire health centre is ruined, all the windows are shattered. And thus they kept standing there for a while, and before they said: Let's go to this other place, to the other scene and see how much damage there is. The man that I didn't know among them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The statement has been tendered. We're now going through this process of eliciting supposedly further evidence in chief from the statement. I don't think it's appropriate in those circumstances that the witness has the statement in front of him and is apparently reading from it at various points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask just a few more questions, Your Honour, and I think we'll be finished with him and he won't need to read from his statement about what I want to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if you perhaps could put the statement a bit on the side and answer the questions from Mr. Hannis without further reading your statement, Mr. Fazlovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, let me ask you about the mosques in Brcko. How many were there that you know of?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four mosques in the town itself. In fact, in the town itself, there were three in the centre of town, and they were blown up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what were the names of the three or how were those three described?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was called the Savska mosque because it was close to the Sava River, another one was called Bijela, or "white mosque" because it was white, and the third was known as the wooden mosque because it was made of wood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall which one was blown up first on that day?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first to be blown up was the Savska mosque, followed by Bijela, and the wooden mosque was the last, within 15 minutes all three of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the first one was blown up but before the second and third one were blown up, I understand from your statement that someone told you the other two were going to go. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. One of my friends, one of my Serb friends who were working with me, told me that. And there was another indication of this; namely, my mother-in-law lived in a building close to the fire station. My mother-in-law is Croat. All the other apartments had windows taped over, and she did not tape her windows in time, because she didn't know that this would happen. She didn't protect her windows from shattering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of the people who lived in the apartments whose windows were taped up?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no more questions for this witness at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Ms. Loukas, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, you'll now be examined by counsel for the Defence. Please proceed. Cross-examined by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, I think you indicated that on the 1st of May - this is in your statement at paragraph 3 - that the JNA came to the fire brigade and you were not mistreated by them. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army troops did not mistreat us, but they didn't let us go home that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think that you indicated in your evidence yesterday that they spoke kindly to you, that "they kindly asked us not to leave the building."

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They explained nicely that they were the Yugoslav People's Army, that they were there to prevent bloodshed, and that we had to stay in the fire station. Yes, they spoke nicely, but they didn't let us go home. They told us we had to stay there, and they did it nicely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you've also indicated that you were -- in your statement, that you were detained at the fire station until the 15th of September, 1992. That's at paragraph 44 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. It was 12 years ago. But a month or so before I was exchanged, I was in the fire station for the whole time, and I was unable to go home, because my home was not fit for -- as a residence any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that you were detained at the fire station until the 15th of September, 1992. Who was detaining you at the fire station?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the so-called labour obligation, or the work obligation. That's the reason why we had to stay there. We had beds inside. However, the Serb colleagues were able to go home and work their normal shifts, whereas we had to sleep there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the situation was that you say you were detained there as a result of a work obligation, but only the Muslim fire-fighters had to stay there as a result of this work obligation; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The whole time, 24 hours a day. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone at the fire brigade keeping you there?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean -- where do you think I was able to go? I didn't rightly understand. I don't understand your question when you say was anyone preventing you from going away, from going out. Serbs were all around and my life would be in danger had I gone out into the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get you to explain to the Court what you mean by "detained at the fire station," which you've got in your statement at paragraph 44.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is we had to stay inside. We were told that we should stay there as long as it is necessary. Nobody said in so many words: "You have to be here." But that was implied. It went without saying. When the work obligation was proclaimed, and even before, it didn't cross our minds to go out into the street, because it was dangerous. That place was the safest place for me as a Muslim, because people, for the most part, didn't even know that I was a Muslim as long as I was doing my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Fazlovic, you indicate in your statement that certain gentlemen came to the fire department; Blagojevic, Stankovic, and Dragan. And I think you've indicated there that Dragan looked almost retarded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think at another point you've indicated that Ranko - this is at paragraph 29 - at one point gave you the impression that he was a lunatic.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have a look at that paragraph 29?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no objection --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please. It's a short paragraph. If you could please read it, Mr. Fazlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Paragraph 29 does not say that it was Ranko who said this man was a lunatic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, Mr. Fazlovic. My question --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that Ranko told me that that man was a lunatic, and we are referring to that man Dragan. I don't know if Ranko knew him at all. I don't see any reference to him here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, I'll just read my question to you again exactly the same question: "And I think at another point you've indicated that Ranko - this is at paragraph 29 - at one point gave you the impression that he was a lunatic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question, of course, is not quite clear, that if you say "he was a lunatic," it could refer to the person earlier described or to Ranko himself. It's ambiguous, the question. So I think you are -- the question of Ms. Loukas is whether you described Ranko at one point to be -- that he seemed to be a lunatic to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand now. I understand. I thought the lady was asking about this other man Dragan. Yes, in one situation, Ranko did appear to me very, very odd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Fazlovic. Now, Mr. Fazlovic, I think you understand the distinction between evidence that you've actually experienced yourself, something you saw or heard or experienced yourself, on the one hand, and indirect evidence or hearsay evidence, something you've heard from someone else. Do you understand that distinction?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference between things that I experienced myself and those that I only heard about, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. Now, Mr. Fazlovic, you've got your statement in front of you. If you'd like to go to page 6 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'll see in that particular paragraph that -- paragraph 23. That's the first paragraph on page 6 in the English version. I'm not sure if paragraph 23 is on page 6 in the B/C/S version. Have you got that particular paragraph, 23?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the paragraph that starts: "When the war began in Croatia"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. Now, you see there that you say that: "Two or three months before the war began in Brcko, a young Serb soldier, Pedja Bojanic, formed a special unit which was attached to the JNA." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fazlovic, the situation is that that's something you've heard about as opposed to being something you can give direct evidence about.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's something I heard about. Of course I wasn't a member of that unit, and I don't have any inside knowledge of what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at page 7 of the English version - that's paragraph 34 - have you found that in the B/C/S version, Mr. Fazlovic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paragraphs are a bit different in different versions. Is this the one that begins with "I also saw Ranko, Miso, and Pero"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. Now, you'll see in there a sentence: "The Republic of Srpska had ordered that all military groups go under the joint command of the republic." Do you see that sentence there?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, that's something you heard about as opposed to being something you can give direct evidence about?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard from this friend I had, Nikolic. But it was no secret. It was known, because all units had to go to the front line, including the units that were under the work obligation, and this also applied to my unit, to the fire brigade, whose staff also had to go to the front line because they were short of people, short of men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Fazlovic, but again, this is not something you can give direct evidence about, but something that you've heard from other people. And you'd agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I could have direct, firsthand knowledge about it. This is something I could only have heard about. Most people know about it the same way. But I also received my own orders concerning the work obligation at the time as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving along to another topic, Mr. Fazlovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If I might have a moment, Your Honour. Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, you indicate that -- you indicate in your statement and you indicated in your evidence today that in June or July you gave certain evidence in relation to the mosques. You recall giving that evidence today?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated, both in your statement and in your evidence today, that there was a man in camouflage uniform when you got there who basically said words to the effect of: Do not put out the fire, just make sure it doesn't spread to other buildings. Do you recall that part of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that man very well. His arms were in bandages. But he was not alone there at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think in your -- you've indicated that the way he treated other Chetniks - that's the word you used - "gave me the impression he was in charge." So the reason you felt he was in charge was the way he treated other Chetniks; is that basically the situation?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that he happened to be in charge there and then. I believe that his soldiers were stationed at the Zaim Musanovic elementary school, that school being located right across the street from the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not from the police station. It's from the mosque.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies from the interpreter. The witness is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But could he, at the same time, be asked to slow down and move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, the interpreters ask you to come a bit closer to the microphone, and thank you for making this correction. The interpreters do their utmost best to translate every word as exact as possible, but it's human to make a mistake now and then, and I see that you're following the English translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fazlovic, so the reason that you thought he was an officer was the impression that you'd formed that he was in charge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impression that he was in charge is because he shouted to the soldiers who were there, he asked them: Why didn't you wait for me to tell you to do it? Apparently they were too early to react and that is why he said that. That's the basis for my assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The basis for your assumption being that he was shouting at people, as you've just said. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He shouted at the soldiers, and only a superior can shout at his men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this was a gentleman you'd never previously seen before, Mr. Fazlovic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... who he was?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and he was a man wearing a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of the soldiers wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty about others - my memory has faded somewhat - but I remember him wearing a camouflage shirt. It was summertime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you remember him wearing a camouflage shirt but you don't remember what he was wearing on the bottom?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing a complete camouflage uniform, but not with a jacket. He only had camouflage trousers and camouflage shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the mosque, you've indicated that you stood in the street next to the truck. And I take it that was right next to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right there in the street. The mosque was on the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you there at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about an hour, an hour and a half, until the fire came down a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in metres, how far were you from the mosque where you were standing for that hour and a half or so?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 20 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And obviously, during that period, your attention was, of course, as a fire-fighter, on the fire.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for us to pay our attention to the fire because that's what they told us not to do. We just came closer a little bit. We were standing there near the health centre, just for appearances' sake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, weren't you told: Do not put out the fire. Make sure it does not spread to the medical centre or other buildings? So to ensure that it didn't spread to other buildings, you'd have to keep your eye on the fire, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we were told. However, the mosque is separated by the street and the health centre parking lot from other buildings. There were about 20 metres -- there was a distance of 20 metres between the mosque and the next house. There was practically no need for us to be there because the fire could not easily spread to the surrounding buildings. But yes, we were told to watch for the fire not to spread to the nearby buildings, but I, as a fire-fighter, knew that the fire could not spread so I just stood there with others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Watching the fire?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Watching the fire, the people around me, the health centre, the soldiers who were standing across the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you were standing there near the health centre just for appearances' sake. Do you recall saying that in answer to a question in the last five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said I was there in the vicinity of the mosque, in the vicinity of the health centre. Yes, I was present. I had been called to come and put down the fire, however, we were not permitted to put out the fire. And the remainder of the time we spent standing there observing. I didn't know what to do. Because I was perfectly aware that it was not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. possible for this fire to spread to the health centre. I was there for no reason, because I was not there to put out the fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for appearances' sake, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that Ms. Loukas is seeking confirmation of that earlier answer. But I do not mind, but would you please come to your point, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For appearances' sake, Mr. Fazlovic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. What is it that you want from me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... confirm that you've said today, within the last five minutes, that you were standing there for appearances' sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the record speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the English translation, Mr. Fazlovic, we read that you said: "We are standing there near the health centre just for appearances' sake." Ms. Loukas would like to know whether that is exactly what you said. She -- as you are aware, your words are translated and she seeks verification that those were your words.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the witness said in Serbo-Croat "reda radi."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try to explain. We had been called to intervene; however, we were not allowed to intervene. We were told initially that we should be there so that the fire would not spread to the health centre and the neighbouring houses that were some 30 or 40 metres away. On the other side of the mosque there was the street, so there was no danger for the fire to spread. So in my opinion, it seemed to me that we were there pro forma, for appearances' sake, because we were simply standing there without being able to perform any duty whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Fazlovic, you'd have to agree, wouldn't you, that a group of fire-fighters standing around while the building burns down isn't much of an appearance for a group of fire-fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I don't understand the relevance. It's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, of course the expression "for appearances' sake" is not very clear, and therefore, to ask the witness whether you'd -- I think he explained several times now what he meant by "for appearances' sake," and that it is that they were there but were not able to do anything. Your question suggests, however, that it's not a big appearance of a fire-fighter doing nothing. Whatever the witness would answer to that question would make not that much of a difference for our understanding of the testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I withdraw that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, getting on to the situation you found yourself in there. There was burning and damaged buildings; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were lots of people around?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Where? Where do you mean that there were a lot of people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were standing around watching the mosque, still next to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was only the mosque that was on fire. I didn't say that other buildings were on fire. You misquoted my words. I don't know why. It was only the mosque that was ablaze. Other buildings only had shattered windows and roofs that had been damaged in the detonation. Soldiers were in the yard of the Zaim Musanovic house. There was a couple of soldiers right next to the mosque. I identified one of them in my statement. Afterwards, gentlemen from the municipality, from the SDS, arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In any event, there was a burning building and there were damaged buildings nearby; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque was burning, and the buildings around the mosque only had damaged windows, damaged glass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, the mosque is burning, you've got some damaged buildings, damaged in the sense that the windows were broken, you've got a lot of people around; agree with all of that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a lot of noise?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, because the soldiers, who were the most numerous, were right across the street, in the yard. We were quite alone on the side over there. I mean we the fire-fighters. A soldier would come closer from time to time and comment something with respect to the fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've got a lot of people around, but there's not a lot of noise; is that what you're saying, Mr. Fazlovic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want -- are you trying to say that there were people around me, around the place where I was standing, or in the vicinity? In the vicinity, yes; some 60 to 70 metres away, there were soldiers who were located at the elementary school, Zaim Musanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So only soldiers around, not any other people, is what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when we arrived, only soldiers. It was only later that the people from the municipality, whom I referred to, arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there weren't any other people around at all other than the soldiers you have referred to and the people from the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just us, the fire-fighters. That part of the town had been vacated, or cleansed. There was no one actually living in that neighbourhood at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, you say that these people from the municipality turned up in a car and then they parked the car. I take it they parked the car several metres away from where you were, at least.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They parked right next to the fire-engine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They parked right next to the fire-engine?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away were they from you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say you heard this conversation, Mr. Fazlovic. Obviously they weren't speaking to you, were they?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a conversation that they had amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And being absolutely fair, Mr. Fazlovic, you'd have to agree that you could not, obviously, hear all of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Why not? It was taking place right next to me. I could hear very well what I just told you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated in your statement that they got out of the car and Ristanic said to Nedjo and another man: Too much explosives were put here, et cetera. Now, obviously you're saying that conversation occurred when -- the minute they got out of the car. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was the minute or two minutes after they got out of the car. I don't see any importance of that. I know what they said. I was present when they said that. It was Djordje Ristanic who made this comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying. But you'd agree with me that it was very soon after they got out of the car, according to your evidence.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When they got out of the car, they observed the situation, and then they started talking about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, so for all you know, the fact is that they could have been saying in the car: If some idiot or fanatic is going to be stupid enough to blow up the mosque, and then the rest of the conversation followed, for all you know. You'd have to agree with that, to be fair, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, the conversation in the car could have been about opera, about the war, about whatever. Let's just seek to hear from the witness what he heard, and all the rest is speculation, unless you have any better source for it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So obviously, Mr. Fazlovic, you can't speculate as to what conversation immediately preceded that conversation that you say you heard. You'd agree with that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they talked about before, before that? I have no idea what they had talked about before, but I know exactly what they said then and there, when I was present. I can repeat their words if you want me to, but I again have no idea what they had discussed before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no need for you to repeat what they said. Just briefly,

utterances.speaker: MR. FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: This statement that you gave to the Prosecution I think took two days, did it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the 14th and 15th of March, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure about the year; however, I'm not a hundred per cent sure about the date. The date, it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, it took two days to give your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I gave the statement in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many hours per day were you doing on the statement on those two days that you were giving the statement to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that it was not two full days. It could have been maybe for two or three hours, but I'm not sure. I know that we had breaks and that we would start again. I really cannot remember the details and tell you how many hours I spent giving the statement in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, it was several hours spread over two days.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think two or three hours per day for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And obviously you were given a chance to read your statement before you signed it.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked if it was true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked if you had anything to add.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fazlovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the Prosecution could provide Mr. Fazlovic with an unblocked-out copy of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, could you assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm just checking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I only have an English copy that's not blocked out.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- oh, unless the time. It's probably time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on -- if you say -- how much time would you still need, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Not that long, I must say, but I may as well just get -- no. Unfortunately, that's also a blacked-out copy. I just need an unblacked-out copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say you need more than -- I'd say more than seven minutes, if we could not finish by 25 minutes to 11.00, and we would have to have a break anyhow. Apart from that, we still have to deal with the Treanor exhibits, which will take us some time because of the complexity of some of the very similar documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can indicate this: I will finish very shortly, but in any event we have to go through the Treanor exhibits so we may as well take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that's a good idea, that we have a break now, that you'll prepare for the unblocked copy of the document. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I take it that now a B/C/S version of the unblocked statement is there for the witness to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Witness [sic]. In fact, I had an unblocked version but it wasn't stapled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not mind if you say "Your Witness," but "Your Honour" is more usual. Even on the transcript it says "Your Honour," but I think as a matter of fact that the interpreters saved. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure what brought that forward, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Let's not discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now -- and Your Honour, I was just about to indicate Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that -- in fact, I had an unblacked copy but it wasn't stapled and I thought it might be a little unwieldy for the witness. But I now have an unblacked-out copy to present to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there are just smaller portions to be read, we could do it this way. If there are, however, bigger portions, then it might be a good idea to tender the unblocked -- or at least the part unblocked as well. But perhaps if there's another copy of the unblocked, then we could perhaps put that on the ELMO so that we could read it together with the witness. Copies for everybody. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can indicate there probably won't be any need to have a copy on the ELMO as such, I wouldn't have thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fazlovic, you'll recall that just prior to the break, I was asking you about your statement that you gave on the 14th and 15th of March, 1995. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you agreed that everything you'd said in that statement was the truth?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that it was a detailed statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That it had taken several hours?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was given over two or three hours per session, for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So it took several hours.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you agreed that you'd had a chance to read the statement before signing it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked if it was true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And asked if you had anything to add.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have a copy, I think, before you of the unblocked-out statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fazlovic, when you were giving evidence yesterday - this is at page 69 of yesterday's evidence, for the benefit of the Court - in answer to a question: "Were there times when you went out on official fire-fighting business during that time?" Your answer was: "Yes. Whenever we were called, either from the police or from the barracks, we went on fire-fighting business, usually extinguishing fire in Muslim houses. But whenever we went there, they would tell us: Why have you come here? Why are you extinguishing fire in these Muslim houses? Although there were Serbs in the unit, there were Serb soldiers, and in 90 per cent of the cases, they would eventually prevent us from putting out the fire. Only if the house in question was a Muslim house but in the vicinity of a Serb house, then they would let us protect this other house." Now, Mr. Fazlovic, you have your statement before you. Show me where in your statement it says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to save time, I'm willing to agree that's not in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just trying to find the transcript of yesterday. I couldn't find it on my computer, so I have to --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I gave the reference, Your Honour. It was the bottom of page 69 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't got it in front of me, so that's my problem. Yes. You've heard what Mr. Hannis said. Is there -- Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Fazlovic, it says nothing in your statement about that; you'd agree with that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say a few words here. If I were to give a full, complete statement, it would take three days, perhaps, because every day that I spent in that unit would take a day to recount. I couldn't put it all in the statement. There were a lot of other ugly things that I experienced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, at page 70 of the evidence you gave yesterday, you indicated that: "Before the 4th of May, nobody mistreated us. But on the 4th of May, at around 8.00, we heard explosion coming up from the yard of the firehouse."

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... "Out through the window, we saw a group consisting of 50 to 60 people who had fired from an RPG. They then rushed into the firehouse."

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fazlovic, again, you've got your statement before you. Where in your statement, if you might show me, does it state that "a group of -- consisting of 50 to 60 people who had fired from an RPG rushed into the firehouse"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, to save time, I'm willing to agree that that is not in his statement. His statement only says that on the 4th of May some men came into the fire station and asked for their identification cards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In view of this, you may ask questions on the basis of the absence of any such statement -- of any such detail in the statement of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Fazlovic, you'd agree, would you not, that that does not appear in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did give a larger statement than the one in front of me, and it struck me during the proofing session before I came to testify that this incident is missing from this one, and I did describe it in detail in my conversation with the Prosecutor. When I gave this statement, I described things at length, and the gentleman who took the statement wrote down only the most important details. However, this particular incident, as described here, is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Fazlovic, you agreed with me that the giving of this particular statement took place over two days and took several hours. We agreed on that earlier. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's answered this two or three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This question has been put to you several times, and it has been consistently answered by the witness. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And obviously, Mr. Fazlovic, the -- when you gave your statement in 1995, it was much closer to the events than we are today.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're saying that your memory improves with age since 1995; is that what you're saying, Mr. Fazlovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That misinterprets his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, the witness has just testified not that his memory improved over the years, but not every detail that he included in his statement when talking to those who put it down on paper is reflected in the document. So therefore, it's a misrepresentation of what the witness said. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fazlovic, you're not saying, are you, that you weren't given an opportunity, when you signed your statement, not to add anything if anything was missing, are you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read my statement and I signed it. However, they reflected only the details that they deemed necessary. There were many other things that they may not have thought interesting enough to include.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who do you say is "they"?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the officer who took down my statement in Tuzla. He focused on certain segments of my statement that could be of use to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that it's the officer's fault that everything is not down here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what I said. I did not say that it was his fault. He knows his job, and I, on my part, gave my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying you told him these details, but he didn't record them. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have a clarification as to which details? He said he did give some details pertaining to one event, but on another event, he said he wasn't asked about, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas. Would you rephrase your question, in view of this observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fazlovic, it's been conceded by the Prosecution, and I think you saw that in Court just now, that there's nothing in your statement about the 50 or 60 people who had fired from an RPG rushing into the firehouse, and that you were told not to put out fires in Muslim houses. You also saw the Prosecutor concede that. Now, do you agree that they're missing from your statement, firstly?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agreed that it's not in the statement. However, it did happen. You can understand it as you choose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Fazlovic, are you saying that you told the officer at the time that the statement was being taken, these things, but that that officer chose not to put them in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly these details. I know that I told him about a great number of things, and I don't know what he chose to write down at the moment. I think I explained at great length how they came to the fire station, how we heard an explosion. I just want to say that only this group of people came into the fire station. I don't know where the rest of them had gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fazlovic, prior to giving -- coming into Court yesterday to give evidence, you obviously spoke with people from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell them that things were missing from your statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not tell them, but of course there are things missing. I just told you a moment ago that I had spent five or six months there that were terrible, and it would take me months to recount all these things here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you were having the conversation with the Prosecution prior to giving evidence, did you -- and you've already said you didn't tell them that there were things missing, did you recall that there were things missing?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even at this moment I could tell you a lot of things that are not in the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, do you consider it important that you were told, you say, not to put out fires in Muslim houses? Do you think that's an important thing?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Important to whom?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Important to you giving your statement.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is common knowledge that Muslim houses, if they had already been set on fire, were not allowed to be saved. Of course, if somebody set the house on fire, they would also prevent you from putting out that fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in any event, that aspect was not put in your statement approximately three years after the event, but was given in evidence here yesterday, approximately 12 years after the event.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention that, and I can mention any number of things that are not in the statement and that are perhaps even more important. I can mention that I found dead people in basements and pulled them out, in the presence of the police. I can tell you any number of things that are not here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fazlovic, you also gave evidence that - today - that Muslims were collected into buses and taken to Batkovic camp. Do you recall giving that evidence today?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show me where in your statement it says that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, we will agree that that is not in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed on the basis of the absence of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. such an element in the statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you'd agree, Mr. Fazlovic, that that's not in your statement but you gave evidence of it today?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not in the statement, but it happened in my town, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Fazlovic, in relation to this question of the mosques, you've indicated that Serb houses had taped their windows. Now, show me where in your statement it says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed on the basis of the absence of such an element in the statement, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Fazlovic, I take it you concede that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concede that we should continue or what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concede that that is yet another thing that you've left out of your statement that was taken three years after the event and you gave evidence of it today, 12 years after the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, whether it's "left out of the statement" is a very unclear expression.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether he said it, whether it was not taken. On the other hand, the witness said that he had no clear recollection on what details he actually gave at that time, so it might be a bit of a difficult exercise to find out whether he said it and it was not taken or whether he didn't say it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Fazlovic, we have these four things that -- these four important things, you'd agree; is that correct, that you've left out of your statement, your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, we agree it's not in the statement. We're not agreeing that he left it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. I take that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Fazlovic, we have these four important things that are not recorded in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which four important things?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The four things that the Prosecution have conceded today and you've conceded today, the four things being -- if you want me to take you through them, I shall. Firstly, we have the question of Batkovici and the buses, number 1; number 2, we have the 50 to 60 people firing from an RPG, rushing to the firehouse, that's number 2; number 3 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you looking for the tapes on the windows, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 3 is the tapes on the windows; and number 4 is not being allowed to extinguish fires at Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that it is not in the statement, but I am even now under oath and I believe that if I state something, that that is equally my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, are you saying that you told these four things to the people who took your statement back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any more whether I did or didn't, or whether I explained these things to them using different words, in another form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the two days that took to give your detailed statement, you failed to mention these four things. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection. That mischaracterises his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the two days that it took to have your detailed statement taken back in 1995 for, as you've said, two to three hours per day, you can't remember whether you mentioned these matters or not.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I described many things, and only when I was exchanged at the police station I recounted these things, and I don't know any longer what I said and when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Fazlovic, prior to giving evidence, you attended a proofing session with the Prosecution lawyers here?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you tell them that four things were missing from your statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not tell them. But regarding many of these points, many of these paragraphs, I gave them a more detailed explanation as compared to what is stated here in the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you tell them about the things that you told us in Court yesterday and today, specifically regarding these four things?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember what you told --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we went through this statement, and I don't remember all the details any more. I spoke at great length about all the things that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't remember -- well, first of all, I withdraw that. What day was it when you attended the proofing session with the Prosecution prior to giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the day after my arrival here. I don't know -- I think it was Saturday, last Saturday. I arrived on Friday and I had the proofing session on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And how long did you spend in the proofing session?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a long time. It was over very soon. We just went through the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Maybe an hour, hour and a half. [Interpretation] Maybe an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
