utterances.text: Sorry. You're saying it was maybe an hour, half an hour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said an hour, an hour and a half, approximately, because I wasn't looking at my watch, and I don't have a watch, by the way. I was brought from the hotel, had the proofing session, and it was over very soon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying the proofing session took about an hour and a half and was over very soon; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection. He's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, you've now changed 60 to 90 minutes into 30 to 60 minutes, that it was soon over, I think the witness has --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- Your Honour, and I appreciate that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you please come to your point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak at great length?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's covered by his previous answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, we are invited not to speak at the same time. I draw your attention to that. And I take that point for myself as well. I ask you to come to your point and not to repeat previous questions that have already been answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fazlovic, you've said in the last five minutes that the proofing session was over very soon, and also that you spoke at great length. Do you agree with me that that's contradictory?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection. That's argumentative, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, is it a correct understanding of the Chamber that you want to draw our attention to the fact that the witness -- that certain elements of what could have been the statement of the witness as it appears on paper are not part of it and that one could wonder why he didn't tell it at that time or why he didn't insist on putting it on paper at that time; and at the same time, you want to draw our attention to the fact that during the proofing session before this testimony in this Court, that he could have asked specific attention to that, he could have discussed that, he could have drawn attention to it, especially after reading his statement? If that is what you'd like to bring specifically to the attention of the Chamber, you've succeeded in doing so. If there's anything else, you may ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I did -- and I think Your Honour's formulation is correct, and that -- Your Honour, what I seek to achieve is to demonstrate to the Court that there's an air of unreliability, therefore, in relation to the witness's statement and evidence. And I don't think there's anything further I need to ask the question [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand that. When I used the rather neutral wording of drawing the Court's attention to a certain aspect, of course it was understood that the consequences had to be drawn out of it, looked at from the perspective of the Defence. So that was clear to the Chamber. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I don't believe there's -- I'm happy to end the cross-examination there, Your Honour. I've covered the points I need to cover and perhaps laboured them a little, but I felt it was important to draw them out for the witness's benefit and for the Court's benefit. I hoped to get his agreement on various matters, and without agreement, one is, unfortunately, forced to further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not blaming you for it, but I just wanted to indicate that, as far as we understand, that we understood your point and it's become quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is there any need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions on redirect. I don't know if Defence counsel wants to proffer the unredacted versions of statements now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the four points not appearing in the statement -- do we need the unredacted statement in order to establish that they are not in? I think it's agreed between the parties that the four points you mentioned; Batkovici camp, not extinguishing the fire, the 50 people that run in, and the taping of the windows, these were the four points, that they do not appear in the statement, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Including the RPG, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, including. But I think that is sufficiently clear even without tendering the unblocked statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we mainly can see from it is that it's not in there where it appears in the transcript of the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. As far as I'm concerned, we have the agreement from the Prosecution that those matters do not appear in the statement and I don't think there's any point in tendering a document just to prove that it doesn't contain something when you have a concession from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we do agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I should like to ask you a very brief question. I actually need some clarification. In your statement -- I don't know whether you have it in front of you, but I'm referring to paragraph number 30. You stated, and I quote from your statement in English, paragraph 30, again, three last lines. You say the following [In English]: "... I saw Nikolic. I asked him, 'Please tell Ranko to leave me alone.' Nikolic said, 'You know I dare not tell Ranko anything. He does not hesitate to kill a Serb.'" [Interpretation] Did you want to say that he didn't even hesitate to kill a Serb? [In English]: "He does not hesitate to kill a Serb." [Interpretation] Does that mean -- I mean, have you understood my question, that he did not hesitate to kill even a Serb?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If such a Serb would try to protect a Muslim. That's the meaning of what I declared there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fazlovic, I have one or more questions for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you as well. You told us that you -- the formation of the special unit, you remember your testimony about that, and when questioned by the Defence, you said that of course you had no direct knowledge of the formation of this unit because you were not part of that unit. Could you tell us from whom you learned that such a formation was established, such a unit was --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This unit consisted of, among others, Ranko, Pedja, and Misa, and I heard in a conversation that I had with Ranko that he was a member of this unit that had been in Vukovar and elsewhere. At that time, the war was not yet going on in Bosnia, but they appeared again once the war broke out in Bosnia. This is what I heard. I was good friends with Pedja's cousin, and I know that this Goran Markovic, who later became a police commander in Brcko, told me that Pedja had been the organiser. I don't know exactly what he did, but at any rate, he was the one who had assembled them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it's clear from your statement that Ranko told you about what he did, or at least that he was part of that unit, but this is how you learned that the unit was then --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the formation of the unit then took place. Yes. Then I have one more question. You said that you had to stay in the building of the fire-fighters. You had to sleep there, you had to stay there, you couldn't leave it, whereas your Serb colleagues could. Has it ever happened that someone asked leave to go out of the building for whatever reason, or did any one of your Muslim colleagues ever try to leave that building, and what then happened, if it happened at all?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It happened from time to time that we left the building. That is true. But this was our place of residence during that period of time. We couldn't go home. We could go out to the shop, for instance. For example, my mother-in-law lived in the vicinity of the firehouse, and I was able to visit her from time to time, but very briefly, for half an hour or so. My wife was no longer in the town. She was already in Serbia. We could go -- we could leave the building and go very short distances. That was possible, but we could not leave for good. We had to sleep there. We had to be present in the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Listening to your answer and looking at your statement that you said you were detained, do I understand well that it was not a strict detention situation where you were strictly confined to the premises, but that you were supposed to return after you briefly left the firehouse? I tried to understand how limited you were in your movements.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have guards watching over us. We were there pursuant to specific orders whereby we were ordered to stay there and perform our work obligation. However, since it was not recommended to walk around the town, because various groups moved around and took people away, we did not want to expose ourselves to that situation. We did not want to stay outside for very long. So whenever -- but whenever we needed to go and do something, we could go out briefly, and then we would go back. So there were no guards, strictly speaking; however, it was not really recommended to go out, for reasons of our personal safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand that you were not quite unhappy with the fact that you were ordered to stay in the firehouse, because it wasn't safe outside anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the safest place for us at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one other question for you. You were asked whether you had any direct knowledge of people being sent to the front lines, and then you said, well, you had no direct knowledge of that, apart from that you, as a fire-fighter, got your orders as well in a similar way. You also told us that your Serb colleagues had to follow their orders. Did you observe yourself that orders given to them, of which you had no direct knowledge, were followed by them, observing this through what you saw them to do?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the very beginning, our colleagues were very kind to us, and they helped us. However, as time went by, they turned away from us. Later, all Serbs working at the fire station received automatic weapons, just in case. I don't know what purpose they were supposed to use it for. We were far away from the centre. They performed their duty the same way as we did; they went to assist with the fire, if this is what you have in mind, what the duties of the fire unit were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also had in mind that you said that they were sent to the front because they had not sufficient people there.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because one day they received call-up papers to go to the front, to the front line. I think they stayed there for about three days. I don't remember exactly how long. And only Muslims remained at the fire station. After the second time when they came back, they threatened us and they said: If they should ever find us again here at the fire station, that they would slaughter us. They were probably afraid because they had to go to the front, and they also probably thought that because if we had not been there, they would not have been sent to the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see these call-up papers, or were you told that they received them?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw when they received the call-up papers at the fire station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers, Mr. Fazlovic. If the questions of the Bench do not raise any -- do not trigger any new questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Just one question arising from your question. Further cross-examination by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, in relation to paragraph 23 of your statement that His Honour asked you about, that was about -- and I'll just go to it briefly so -- oh, you've got the statement in front of you. "When the war began in Croatia, Ranko joined the JNA. When I saw him, he said he was in the army, that his salary was good, and that he did not have to do anything. He said he went to Vukovar. Two or three months before the war began in Brcko, a young Serb soldier, Pedja Bojanic, formed a special unit which was attached to the JNA." You remember that paragraph in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you think you might be wrong about any of that, Mr. Fazlovic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you change your answer if I told you that Mr. Cesic has been sentenced by this Court and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Yes. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you change your answer if I told you that Mr. Cesic has been sentenced by this Tribunal and it was there indicated that he had no military career prior to May 1992? Would you change your answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm referring to page 11 of the sentencing judgement, Your Honour, the Ranko Cesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not change my answer, because I know he was active. I know Ranko personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Then, Mr. Fazlovic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you for having come a very far way, for having answered all the questions by both parties and by the Bench, even now and then in English, and even correcting us, once on an answer you gave in B/C/S but that was translated in English. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Your Honour. It's been a pleasure for me to assist to the Court in finding the right solution to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fazlovic. Madam Usher, you may escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, I'd like to start with the exhibits in relation to this witness, Mr. Fazlovic, first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P71, the witness statement of Mr. Fazlovic; and P71.1, the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's the blocked version of his statement as it was distributed today, and not the one we started distributing yesterday. It's admitted into evidence. Could we then, please, turn to the exhibits that were tendered during the testimony of Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P64, expert report of Patrick Treanor, in English; P64.1, B/C/S translation. P64A, 28 binders of footnotes to the expert report of Patrick Treanor. P65, 16 binders with 224 tabs. P66, CD video of speeches of Radovan Karadzic and Nikola Koljevic. P66A, transcript of P66 in B/C/S; P66A.1, English translation of P66A. P67, CD of intercepts. P67A, transcripts of intercepts in B/C/S; and P67A.1, English translations. P68, binder of maps and graphs with 21 tabs. P69, CD of video of speech by Radovan Karadzic on 15 October 1991. P69A, transcript of Exhibit P69; and P69A.1, English translation. P70, CD clip of Momcilo Krajisnik explaining the Bosnia and Herzegovina ethnic map. And P70A, transcript of P70 in B/C/S; and P70A.1, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are the Prosecution exhibits. Since I hear no objections, they're admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, the Defence exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibits: D5, the Lisbon Agreement, Statement of Principles for New Constitutional Arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina, in English, signed in Sarajevo March 18th, 1992. D6, the Lisbon Agreement, Statement of Principles for New Constitutional Arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina in B/C/S, signed in Lisbon February 28, 1992. D7, map annexed to Lisbon Agreement signed in Sarajevo in 1992. D8, pages 101, 102, and 103 of book written by Alija Izetbegovic, entitled "Memoirs," in B/C/S. D9, English letter to Mr. Jovicic from Graham Blewitt, dated 30 July 2001, with B/C/S translation. And B/C/S letter in response from Mr. Milovan Bjelica, dated 5 November 2001, and English translation. D10A through D10O, 15 copies of instructions for the organisation and operation of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in emergency conditions. That is the Variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the final list of the exhibits, you'll find from D10A up until D10O, which appears in the transcript more or less as D100, but it's D10-O, you'll find the ERN numbers specified, so in order not to have any confusion at a later stage. So whenever you'd like to refer to one of these documents, and if you're uncertain on which one, whether we have the telefax copy or the number 100 copy, with stamps or without stamps, then please consult the list kept by the Registry, in which you'll find exactly the ERN numbers as they appear on these documents, so in order to avoid whatever confusion. I heard no objections, but I've got one question in respect of D7, and related to D5 and D6. It's my recollection that there was some confusion about sources from the Internet or whatever. Has this been sorted out by the Defence that the copies D5 and D6 are actually the text of the Lisbon Agreement as signed in Sarajevo, and that's D5 and D6 being the Lisbon Agreement as signed in February in Lisbon already?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can indicate in that regard, Your Honour, that my case manager has not at this point finalised her comparisons with -- between the English and the B/C/S versions and the other versions we received from the Prosecution. So that process, of course, has not at this stage yet been finalised. We assume that that could be done on the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And then we could finalise it then, if that would be appropriate to the Tribunal. It's just we felt that it was important to go through the B/C/S version to ensure that the copies were correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, then, although it's not a procedure I like very much, but they are provisionally admitted into evidence, on the basis of the understanding that D5 is the Lisbon Agreement, as signed in March in Sarajevo; and that D6 is the Lisbon Agreement as signed in February in Lisbon itself. And my final question would be about D7. Madam Registrar just read that it was a map annexed to the Lisbon Agreement. I do remember that there was some confusion -- at least some uncertainty about that as well, whether it was really attached to the text, and if so, to which one of these texts. So, therefore, I'd suggest that if we admit D7 into evidence, that we call it "map related to the Lisbon Agreement," which is different from "attached to," and I also perhaps would prefer to provisionally admit them into evidence on the basis of the understanding that this map is actually related to the Lisbon Agreements, or the two versions of the Lisbon Agreement. And the Chamber would appreciate to hear from the Defence within the next two weeks whether the basis upon which we provisionally admitted these documents into evidence is a solid basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, for that indulgence. Yes. We propose -- I think that is the appropriate course, the sort of provisional -- to provisionally admit them at this point, and we will be able to clarify that, I would hope, safely, within the next two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. You're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One small note with respect to D8, which as the Court will recall consisted of excerpts from Mr. Izetbegovic's book. There's still a context related issue. As you know, it's not translated into English. We have no objection to its admission, but we'd like to reserve the opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there is no translation into English, it's not only for the parties to be able to find the context, but these three pages should be accompanied by an English translation, if it's not published in English, rather soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can indicate in that regard, Your Honour, that we've had no final response yet from the translation unit, the CLSS. But we do expect to receive it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you say no final response, that means no translation, or no response whether they could translate it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We were just waiting on a response as to whether the book had already been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, for the record, I indicate that if no English translation of this book exists, that since these pages, three pages, will be admitted into evidence, the translation of those pages should get priority, and with reference to the transcript of this hearing, you may bring this under the attention of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Tieger. If there's nothing else, we adjourn for the day -- no. I first have to admit into evidence the exhibits just mentioned; D5, D6, and D7 provisionally admitted, as I explained before. Having said this, and if there's nothing else to be discussed at this moment, we'll adjourn and we'll be in this same courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of April 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
